title: Parse hotcall outliers investigation notes
content:
Purpose
This is a working scratchpad capturing an investigation into sporadic 'hotcall' CPU outliers we see during tiny-request workloads (single-digit token prompts). Goal: produce a reproducible repro, narrow root causes (parse vs tokenize vs handoff), and list low-risk mitigations we can try in the next sprint.

Background / why this matters
- Tiny requests are a large fraction of interactive traffic for a few customers; 95th/99th tail affects UX.
- Our observability shows intermittent spikes where a single request consumes ~5–15ms CPU on the host outside the expected tokenize+rpc path. These correlate with short request paths but high scheduler/lock contention on flamegraphs.
- Hypotheses: expensive parse branch (header/json), allocator stalls during buffer growth, Python GIL contention in request prep path, or thread-pool handoff jitter (worker parking/unparking).

High-level observations (from traces + sampling)
- Sampling + perf script on a test box (c7g-like emulation): 200k tiny requests over 30m under 1000rps synthetic load. At 99th percentile, stacks frequently show: parse_header->json_parse->PyEval_EvalFrame->park_worker or futex_wait -> kernel.syscall.
- Flamegraphs show a small but visible bucket in our C extension for HTTP header scanning (fastpath) escaping to Python only when boundary conditions hit (long header, weird charset).
- Allocator (jemalloc) statistics during spikes: increases in small allocations and deallocations, with occasional arena contention on cores pinned to same NUMA node.

Microbench experiments run (commands + short results)
1) Isolated header parse microbench (C harness borrowed from request-parse module):
   - Input: 1M headers, avg len 128, 10% malformed-ish (extra CR).
   - Result: mean 10us/header, 99th 45us. When we disable UTF-8 normalization -> 99th drops to 18us.
2) Python-bridge overhead probe: call into Python callback from C parse for boundary detection (tight loop):
   - 1e6 calls: avg 1.4us overhead/call; but when another thread pinned on same core enters CPython bytecode, overhead jumps to 2.7us/call (GIL acquisition jitter).
3) Worker park/unpark jitter replay: synthetic workload that parks worker threads on condition variable, then signals; measure wake latency
   - median wake 2us, 99th 90us on test harness with 32 workers under load. Replacing pthread_cond with eventfd reduces 99th to 6us.
4) Small-allocation behavior: run rapid request object allocate/free using jemalloc stats
   - Observed periodic spikes correlated with arena mutex contention for threads >= 24. Switching to per-thread caches reduced spike magnitude in local tests.

Key root-cause candidates (ranked)
- 1) Worker wake/hand-off jitter (parking/unparking implementation): high confidence. Evidence: spike correlates to park/unpark latency in synthetic and production traces show futex/wake syscalls. Replacing condvar with eventfd shows large improvement.
- 2) Python GIL acquisition jitter on tight bridge paths: medium confidence. Evidence: extra cost when Python threads compete; C callback->Python transition costs amplified under concurrency.
- 3) UTF-8/normalization fallback in header/tokenizer for edge cases: low-to-medium confidence. Costly only when hit, but contributes to 99th in corpora with weird inputs.
- 4) jemalloc arena contention for extremely high worker counts: low confidence but reproducible on specific instance sizes and high concurrency.

Non-root causes (unlikely)
- Network stack or syscall batcher: sampling shows kernel time dominated by futex/wake not send/recv.
- GC pauses: traces don't show long stop-the-world times in Python; incremental overhead small.

Quick experiments we can run next (short-term, low-risk)
- Replace conditional variable handoff for tokenization queue with eventfd-based wake (A/B on canary): implement small wrapper and test under 1k rps tiny workload.
- Add fast-exit for header paths that are pure ascii and length < 64 to avoid normalization. Add tests + fuzz corpus from prod to measure hit rate.
- Add lightweight per-thread request object pool (object recycle) to reduce small allocs; measure jemalloc metrics.
- Instrument GIL acquisition latency histogram near parse -> Python boundary (micro tracer) to get percentiles in prod sampling.

Medium-term changes (requires more review)
- Consider a small C-only tokenizer fastpath that never calls into Python for very small, common headers. This avoids GIL and cross-language overhead at cost of duplicated checksum logic.
- Evaluate switching jemalloc config to more per-thread caching or use tcache-friendly patterns for our alloc profile.

Metrics to collect for decisioning
- Distribution of park/unpark latency (p99, p999) per instance type and core count.
- Frequency of UTF-8 normalization fallback on inbound headers (per-route).
- GIL acquisition latency histogram correlated with lock holder and stack trace.
- jemalloc arena contention events / mutex sleep time.
- End-to-end 99/99.9 latency for tiny requests (baseline and with each mitigation).

Repro steps (how to rerun the main experiments)
1) Checkout the perf-replay harness: github link in linked_artifacts.
2) Build test image with DEBUG_SYSCALLS=1, jemalloc stats enabled.
3) Run: ./bench --mode tiny-req --rps 1000 --duration 1800 --workers 32 --corpus samples/tiny-requests.json
4) Collect: perf record --call-graph dwarf -p $(pidof serving-runtime) during the run; and run /scripts/park-wake-capture.sh to capture futex timings.

Open questions / unknowns
- Are some customer corpora skewing header parsing cost? We should identify routes with higher normalization fallback rates.
- Any OS-level tunables (futex ownership handoff, eventfd tuning) that we can rationalize across instance types?
- Is the worker parking algorithm compatible with our autoscaling/burst patterns (frequent park/unpark sequence when bursty traffic)?

Proposed immediate plan (next 2 weeks)
- Week 1: Implement eventfd wake variant behind a feature flag; run A/B canary on staging; gather wake latency histograms. (Owner: Jonah)
- Week 1: Add ascii-fastpath header check + telemetry (Owner: Sasha)
- Week 2: Per-thread object pool POC and jemalloc stat collection (Owner: Lina)
- Week 2: Add micro-instrumentation for GIL acquisition histogram (Owner: Evan)

Notes & references
- Observed similar patterns in other teams' microservices; they solved with eventfd wakeups and per-thread caches.
- See linked PR for small eventfd wrapper.
- Keep an eye on interaction with SRE changes to cgroup/cpu accounting which may amplify wake latencies.

Appendix: quick sample flamegraph note
- When looking at the flamegraph around 99th samples: stack often appears as
  parse_headers.c:fast_scan -> parse_headers.c:boundary_detect -> pyshim.c:call_slowpath -> PyEval_EvalFrameEx -> futex_wait
  Suggests slowpath into pyshim + GIL + thread park.

End of notes.

(Working doc — expect iterations; will move to RFC once we have clean repro and A/B results.)
